issues.legal_issue: Retrospective validating legislation may neutralize an earlier court judgment when it removes the legal basis on which that judgment rested.
material_facts: An earlier judgment directed that the value of coal in stock before the appointed day be credited to the mine owner in the accounts for the period of government management.
A later amendment, made retrospective, deemed the prescribed compensation to include the value of coal in stock and provided that no further amount was payable for it.
The amendment also addressed the effect of contrary judgments and the legislature's authority to enact the retrospective change was not successfully challenged.
issues.conclusion: The retrospective amendment removed the basis of the earlier judgment and made its direction ineffective; the amendment could validly do so.
issues.legal_principle: Legislatures may enact retrospective legislation within their competence, subject to the Constitution. A validating law may neutralize a court judgment by changing the law's basis, but merely declaring that a judgment does not bind is insufficient: the defect or basis identified by the court must actually be removed. The Court applied Shri P.C. Mills v. Broach Municipality and the related principles in West Ramnad Electric Distribution Co. Ltd. v. State of Madras, Udai Ram v. Union of India, Tirath Ram v. State of U.P., Krishna Chandra v. Union of India, Hindustan Gum & Chemicals Ltd. v. State of Haryana, and Utkal C. & J. (P) Ltd. v. State of Orissa. It distinguished D. Cawasji & Co. v. State of Mysore because the amendment there had not cured the defect underlying the earlier judgment. The Court also noted that the validity of the nationalisation legislation had been upheld in Tara Prasad Singh v. Union of India.

rule.if: challenge_to_retrospective_validating_legislation and prior_judgment_granted_claim and amendment_retroactively_changes_legal_basis and amendment_removes_basis_of_prior_judgment and legislation_within_legislative_competence

predicates.challenge_to_retrospective_validating_le: The proceeding challenges legislation that purports to change the legal position for an earlier period.
predicates.prior_judgment_granted_claim: A court had previously granted a claim under the legal position then in force.
predicates.amendment_retroactively_changes_legal_ba: The legislature made a change that applies to the period and circumstances covered by the earlier judgment.
predicates.amendment_removes_basis_of_prior_judgmen: The change alters the legal basis on which the earlier judgment granted relief.
predicates.legislation_within_legislative_competenc: The legislature had authority to enact the change and no applicable constitutional bar prevented it.

issues.definition: When a challenge concerns retrospective legislation, an earlier judgment granted relief, the legislation applies to the relevant period, the change removes the basis of that relief, and the legislature had authority to enact it, the earlier judgment is rendered ineffective.

issues.legal_issue: The value of coal already in stock at the transition to nationalised ownership is not separately payable or creditable in management-period accounts when the governing retrospective law treats that value as included in compensation.
material_facts: The mine owner retained ownership while the mine was managed by a government-appointed custodian before nationalisation took effect.
Coal extracted during that management period remained in stock immediately before the appointed day.
The earlier judgment had required the stock's value to be taken into account in balancing the management-period accounts.
The retrospective amendment deemed the scheduled compensation to include the value of stock and barred any further payment for it.
issues.conclusion: The stock's value was not separately payable and was not to be taken into account in the management-period accounts.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 10(2), 19 and 22(1) of the Coking Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1972, as amended, the compensation is deemed to include the value of the coal in stock immediately before the appointed day, and no further amount is payable for that stock. The retrospective deeming provision also means the stock's value is not separately included when preparing the management-period accounts under Section 22(1).

rule.if: interim_mine_management_accounting_case and owner_retained_ownership_before_transfer and coal_remained_in_stock_at_transition and governing_law_deems_compensation_to_include_stock

predicates.interim_mine_management_accounting_case: The proceeding concerns accounting for a mine during a period when its management had been taken over before ownership transferred.
predicates.owner_retained_ownership_before_transfer: The mine owner continued to own the mine during the period of government management before the transfer of ownership.
predicates.coal_remained_in_stock_at_transition: Coal extracted from the mine remained unsold immediately before the transfer took effect.
predicates.governing_law_deems_compensation_to_incl: The applicable law treats compensation as already including the value of the coal in stock at the transition.

issues.definition: When an accounting proceeding concerns interim government management, the owner retained ownership until transfer, coal remained in stock at the transition, and the governing law treats compensation as including that stock, its value is not separately payable or creditable.
